entries.title: No home given; Nathanael of Cana

entries.title: “Son of Talmai”

entries.title: J. F. Fenlon, Catholic Encyclopedia
entries.text: “No mention of St. Bartholomew occurs in ecclesiastical literature before Eusebius.” Other traditions send him to Mesopotamia, Persia, Egypt, Armenia, Lycaonia, Phrygia and the Black Sea coast.

entries.title: Later traditions, as summarised by J. F. Fenlon
entries.text: He died at Albanopolis in Armenia: “according to some, he was beheaded, according to others, flayed alive and crucified, head downward”. Fenlon calls the manner of death “equally uncertain”.

cols.label: John 1 · Nathanael, if he is Bartholomew

verses.text: Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.
And Nathanael said unto him, Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, Come and see.
Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!
Nathanael saith unto him, Whence knowest thou me? Jesus answered and said unto him, Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee.
Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.
Now the names of the twelve apostles are these; The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;
Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.
And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder:
And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Canaanite,
And Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him: and they went into an house.
Simon, (whom he also named Peter,) and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew,
Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphæus, and Simon called Zelotes,
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.

And when they were come in, they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James.

claim.text: Jesus answers Nathanael, “thou shalt see greater things than these” (John 1:50).
Named next to Philip in three of the lists (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14). As Nathanael, brought to Jesus by Philip (John 1:45–46).

person.name: Peter, Thomas and the sons of Zebedee

claim.text: As Nathanael, he went fishing with them when the risen Jesus appeared by the sea (John 21:2–3).

family.text: The name Bartholomew means “son of Talmai” (or Tholmai). Fenlon (1907) notes that it may have been his own name, or a family name added to tell him apart.

identifications.text: Bartholomew appears only in the four lists of the Twelve. Nathanael appears only in John’s Gospel (John 1:45–51; 21:2), which never uses the name Bartholomew.
In Matthew, Mark and Luke, Bartholomew is named straight after Philip; in Acts 1:13 Thomas comes between them. In John, Philip is the one who brings Nathanael to Jesus (John 1:45).

The earliest writer found who equates the two is Ishodad of Merv (about 850): “Bartholomew is perhaps Nathanael”, and “It is handed down that Nathanael, that is to say, Bar Toulmi, was well acquainted with the Scriptures”. This page shows both records and treats the identification as a view.

scripture.text: Scripture says nothing of Bartholomew after the upper room (Acts 1:13), or of Nathanael after the morning by the sea (John 21:2).

items.q: Is Bartholomew the same man as Nathanael?
items.full: Is Bartholomew the same man as Nathanael?

argument.text: Its opening list of apostles names Bartholomew and Nathanael as two men. The same list also names Peter and Cephas as two.

views.label: Nathanael was not one of the Twelve

argument.text: Augustine reasons that Nathanael “was learned and skilled in the law and for that reason was the Lord unwilling to place him among His disciples”, because he chose unlearned men.

views.label: The same man: Nathanael, son of Talmai
views.holders: Ishodad of Merv (about 850); generally held from the 9th century on (Kerr, 1915); reasons set out by Fenlon (1907)

argument.text: John never uses the name Bartholomew and the other Gospels never use Nathanael; the Gospel lists pair Bartholomew with Philip, who brought Nathanael; Nathanael was among disciples with apostles in John 21:2. Fenlon calls the case “ingenious and pretty strong”, with the weak link that Nathanael “may have been another personage”.
